newsitem.title: UK: Hidden germs may cause multiple sclerosis-research.
newsitem.headline: Hidden germs may cause multiple sclerosis-research.

text.p: Germs hiding out in the brain, where the body's immune system cannot find them, could be responsible for the nerve disease multiple sclerosis, British researchers reported on Tuesday.

Hugh Perry, a pharmacologist at Oxford University, said animal tests indicated that bacteria or viruses could lurk undetected for months before helping trigger an immune system response against the nervous system.
He told a joint meeting of Britain's Biochemical Society and the British Society for Immunology that he and colleagues had injected killed bacteria into the brains of rats.
The rats' immune systems did not respond. But months later they gave the rats another dose of killed bacteria -- this one into the skin.
This time the immune systems charged up and white blood cells entered the brain to go after the hidden bacteria there.
In attacking the bacteria they damaged blood vessels and the myelin sheath that insulates the nerves -- which is just what happens in MS.

"These and other ongoing experiments have demonstrated that the immune system can be drawn to the brain by bacteria or viruses, and that the immune response against these foreign micro-organisms can lead to "bystander" tissue damage in the brain with similarities to the tissue damage seen in MS," Perry said.
